Recurrent Neural Networks · Part 6

The whole machine

The full Transformer: an encoder that reads, a decoder that writes, and attention joining them. No RNN anywhere.

23 Oct 2026→ encoder × 2→ decoder × 2→ 2026-10-23
Part 5 built self-attention and named one Transformer block. Today we assemble the whole thing from the original paper, piece by piece, and then train it on the same date task as Parts 3 and 4, with the same exam, so we can compare it with the RNN models honestly.

Where we left off

One block, and three open questions

  1. What do the feed-forward, the skip and the norm each do, and why stack N blocks?
  2. How does a decoder built from blocks write an answer, and how does it see the input?
  3. Training sees the whole answer at once; writing can't. How do both work with the same model?
This is Part 5's last diagram. Part 5 explained the attention box in detail and only named the rest. This deck fills in the three questions, in order, then runs the result on the date translator.

The map for today

Encoder on the left, decoder on the right

Redrawn from Figure 1 of Attention Is All You Need (Vaswani and colleagues, 2017).

This is the most famous diagram in deep learning, and the one to be able to draw in an interview. Click through the parts. Two columns, like Part 3: the encoder reads the whole input, the decoder writes the output one character at a time. Three things are new compared with one block from Part 5: the decoder's mask, the cross-attention box in the middle of the decoder, and the output layer on top. The paper uses N = 6 blocks on each side and d = 512; our date model uses N = 2 and d = 64.

The encoder

Embed, add positions, then N identical blocks

1
Embed. Each input character picks its row of a learned table, times √d.
ei = Ein[xi] · √d (68 × 64 table)
2
Add positions, Part 5's sine waves.
zi(0) = ei + pi
3
N blocks, each with its own weights; one block's output is the next one's input.
z(l) = Blockl( z(l−1) ) l = 1 … N
  • Every block keeps the shape: T × d in, T × d out, one vector per input character. The last one is the encoder's output, the memory.
  • Why stack? Block 1 mixes characters. Block 2 mixes those mixtures: “the 2 that sits in a 4-digit group after a month name”. More blocks, more steps of combining.
Compared with Part 4, the memory plays the role of h_1 … h_T: one vector per input position for the decoder to look at. The difference is how it was built: by self-attention over the whole input instead of an RNN reading left to right, so every memory has seen both sides. The √d: embeddings start small, and multiplying by √d brings them to about the same size as the positions, so neither drowns the other (this is the paper's choice). The paper stacks 6 encoder blocks; BERT-base 12; big models 100 or more. Our date model uses 2, which is enough for this task.

Inside a block · 1

Feed-forward: each position on its own

FFN(z) = ReLU( z W1 + b1 ) W2 + b2

Two layers: d → 4d → d. The same weights for every position, but no position sees another.

sizesshare of a block's weights
original Transformer512 → 2048 → 512about ⅔
our date model64 → 256 → 64about ⅔

Attention gathers: it moves information between positions. The feed-forward works on what each position gathered.

Attention on its own is only weighted averaging of value vectors, then one matrix: it can move information around, but it does little computing with it. The feed-forward layer adds the non-linear work, the ReLU, applied to each position separately. "Applied to each position separately" is the paper's own wording; you'll also hear "position-wise". Where the ⅔ comes from: an attention sublayer has 4 d × d matrices (Q, K, V, O) = 4d² weights; the feed-forward has d × 4d plus 4d × d = 8d². So 8 of every 12 weights in an encoder block are in the feed-forward. A common interview claim, worth checking yourself.

Inside a block · 2

Add, don't replace: the residual path

z ← z + sublayer(z)

Each sublayer adds a correction to z instead of replacing it. Stack 12 sublayers and there's still a straight line from the input to the top: the plus signs.

Blame (the gradient) flows back down that line untouched: the derivative of z + f(z) is 1 + f′(z), never just f′. The same trick as the LSTM's belt in Part 2.

From image models: Kaiming He and colleagues, Deep Residual Learning (2015).

sublayers stacked
blame kept per sublayer
no skips
skips: straight path

Blame reaching the bottom layer, as a share of what the top got. Illustrative numbers: each sublayer passes back a fixed share, like Part 2's blame race.

Without the skips, blame reaching the bottom is a product of one factor per sublayer, and a product of many numbers below 1 shrinks fast: the vanishing gradient from Part 2, now across layers instead of time steps. With the skips, one of the paths back is the straight line through the plus signs, which multiplies by 1 at every step, so the bottom always gets at least that share. The "with skips" bar shows that one straight path alone, which passes 100% however deep the stack; the paths through the sublayers add to it. Real networks are messier, but the straight path is why 96-block models train at all. Interview phrasing: "residual connections give the gradient an identity path, so deep stacks train".

Inside a block · 3

Layer norm: a steady scale for every word

After each add, take one word's vector, subtract its own mean and divide by its own spread. Then a learned scale γ and shift β per slot.

LayerNorm(z) = γ ⊙ ( z − mean(z) ) / std(z) + β
multiply by
add
one word's z (8 of its numbers)
after layer norm (γ = 1, β = 0)

Scale or shift the input as much as you like: the output doesn't move. Every block hands the next one numbers of about the same size.

Why it's needed: every residual add makes z a bit bigger, and after many blocks the numbers would drift in size, which upsets softmax (Part 5's √d_k slide) and makes training unstable. Layer norm resets every word's vector to mean 0 and spread 1, and γ and β let the model choose a different scale per slot if that helps. "Layer" norm because it normalises across the d numbers of one word, not across the batch (that would be batch norm, from image models). Introduced by Jimmy Ba, Jamie Kiros and Geoffrey Hinton, "Layer Normalization" (2016). The paper normalises after the add ("post-norm"), as our demo does; most models since GPT-2 normalise before each sublayer ("pre-norm"), which trains more stably in deep stacks. That's the one variant worth knowing by name.

Try it · the real model

One encoder block, step by step

This is block 1 of the trained date model, run in the browser on "23 Oct 2026". Each row is one input character; each column is one of its numbers (rust positive, blue negative). Walk down the stages and say the shape at each one: it starts and ends at 11 × 64, and only grows inside (the four heads' 11 × 11 maps, and the feed-forward's 11 × 256). Things to point out: after the positions are added, the two "2"s have different rows; after layer norm, every row has the same overall strength. The encoder's own attention maps are honestly hard to read: they spread over separators and digits. The clean maps are the decoder's cross-attention, later.

The decoder

Three sublayers instead of two

sublayerqueries fromkeys and values fromlooks at
1masked self-attentionthe answer so farthe answer so faritself and earlier characters only
2cross-attentionthe answer so farthe encoder's memoryevery input character
3feed-forward—nothing: each position alone
  • Each one wrapped the same way: z ← LayerNorm(z + sublayer(z)).
  • Its input is the answer written so far, shifted right: ⟨s⟩ 2 0 2 6 …, so the position that sees “⟨s⟩” must guess “2”.
  • Every decoder block uses the same memory: the encoder runs once, the decoder's blocks all look at its output.
Read the table out loud as the interview answer: "the decoder block is masked self-attention over the output so far, cross-attention to the encoder output, and a feed-forward, each with residual and layer norm". Sublayer 1 is how the decoder remembers what it already wrote: in Part 3 that was the RNN's hidden state; here it's attention over the written characters. Sublayer 2 is how it reads the input. The shift right is the same y_in vs y_out trick from Part 3's demo.

The join

Cross-attention is Part 4 again

Part 4 · GRU + attentionPart 6 · cross-attention querythe decoder's memory st−1, through Wsthe decoder position's vector, through WQ keysevery encoder hj, through Whevery memory vector, through WK valuesevery hj itselfevery memory vector, through WV scorev · tanh(Wss + Whhj)q · kj / √dk, in 4 heads how oftenonce per character writtenonce per decoder block, for every position

Same question as Part 4: “for what I'm about to write, which input characters matter?” Score, soften, mix. Only the score and the plumbing changed.

This is the slide that ties the course together. Bahdanau-style attention between an encoder and a decoder didn't go away in the Transformer; it became the cross-attention sublayer. What's different: the score is the scaled dot product from Part 5, there are several heads, and it happens in every decoder block. If someone asks "where's the attention from the 2014 translation paper in a Transformer?", this is the answer. The maps we'll draw from the demo are the weights of this sublayer.

The top

From a vector to the next character

1
Score every character in the output alphabet against the top decoder vector u.
score(c) = u · ec + bc
2
Softmax the 14 scores into probabilities, as in every part so far.
P(next = c) = softmax(score)c
  • ec is the same row the decoder used to embed character c. The paper shares these weights: one table, used at the bottom to read a character and at the top to score it.
  • Our model: u has 64 numbers, the output alphabet has 14 characters (⟨s⟩, ⟨/s⟩, -, ;, 0–9). With the paper's 37,000-token vocabulary, sharing saves millions of weights.

Weight sharing: Ofir Press and Lior Wolf, Using the Output Embedding to Improve Language Models (2016).

The output layer is the same as in every earlier part: a linear layer then softmax. The weight-sharing detail is a nice interview extra: it says "a good next character is one whose embedding points the same way as u". Our demo shares, like the paper; the encoder has its own table because its alphabet is different.

Training vs writing · 1

Training: the whole answer in one pass

Feed in the right answer, shifted right (Part 3's teacher forcing). The mask stops each position seeing the characters after it.

So one pass of the decoder makes 11 guesses at once, one per row, each from only what came before. 11 losses, one backward pass.

Part 3's GRU decoder had to take 11 steps, one after another, to get the same 11 losses.

This is where the Transformer's training speed comes from. The mask is what makes it legal: without it, the row that's meant to guess "6" could just look at the "6" in the next column. In our demo, Transformer.forward with teacher_forcing=True is one call to the decoder over all positions; the GRU models loop. The hatching is the masked upper triangle from Part 5, now on the real answer. Shading in the allowed cells is illustrative.

Training vs writing · 2

Writing: still one character at a time

Nobody knows the answer yet, so each character must be written before it can be fed back in: one decoder pass per character, as in Part 3.

The real model, writing "23 Oct 2026". Each line is one full run of the decoder on everything written so far; it outputs one new character, which is appended for the next pass. Training is parallel, writing is not: that's true of every Transformer that writes, including chatbots, which is why their answers stream in a word at a time. Real systems don't recompute the earlier positions on every pass: they keep each position's keys and values from earlier passes, the "KV cache". Our demo recomputes, which is simpler and fine for 11 characters. The counter shows how much work that recomputing costs.

Measured

Is it actually faster to train?

One training round (128 inputs, forward and backward), on a laptop CPU, untrained weights:

dates per inputaverage inputPart 4 · GRU + attentionPart 6 · Transformer
119 characters36 ms36 ms
1–451 characters222 ms130 ms
uv run demo/transformer.py speed

On short inputs, a tie. On longer ones the GRU's step-by-step wait shows. On a GPU, which is built for big parallel multiplies, the gap is far larger.

An honest measurement, not a slogan. With tiny models on a CPU, the per-step work is so small that waiting barely matters, so the two tie at one date. The GRU's cost grows with the number of steps it must take in order (input length plus output length); the Transformer's work grows too (T² for attention), but it comes as a few big matrix multiplies. That's Part 5's table, measured: "steps that must wait for each other: T vs 1". Speeds vary by machine; run the command to get your own.

Demo · same task, same exam

The date translator, with no RNN

Same data and exam as Parts 3 and 4. The model: d = 64, 4 heads, 2 encoder + 2 decoder blocks, 238,734 weights (Part 4's had 200,590).

Written out block by block in demo/transformer.py, so every slide so far is a few named lines.

uv run demo/transformer.py train
uv run demo/transformer.py test
uv run demo/transformer.py translate \
  "23 Oct 2026" --details
examPart 4 · GRU + attentionPart 6 · Transformer
dates it never saw · 1900–2079100%100%
years it never saw · 2080–2099, in digits99.9%81.9%
years it never saw · spelled out99.3%99.8%

Perfect on every format and length it was trained on. The surprise is the second row: we'll look at why in a moment.

Numbers from one run each (seed 0) of demo/attention.py test and demo/transformer.py test: 39,444 inputs from unseen days, 43,836 from unseen years. Training took about 2.5 minutes on a laptop CPU, a little longer than Part 4's, mostly because the check on the validation set writes answers one character at a time. Don't oversell the comparison: one seed each, small models, a toy task. The point is that the RNN can be removed entirely and the task still gets solved, and that the models fail in different places.

What to write next?

The trained Transformer, running in the browser. Same picture as Part 4's live slide, but now there are 8 maps: 2 decoder blocks × 4 heads. Start with block 2, "all heads" (the average): it's almost Part 4's map, year first, then back to "Oct" for the month, then to "23" for the day. Then click through the heads of block 2: head 3 is a near-perfect alignment, others are messier and probably carry other information. Block 1's heads are less tidy. Try "Friday, 13 March 2071" and the spelled-out date.

Demo · all eight at once

Eight maps, not one

All 8 cross-attention maps of the trained model for one input: top row block 1, bottom row block 2. Unlike Part 5's heads slide, these are real weights, not illustrative. Some heads are crisp alignments, some are diffuse, some look at the same place as another head. That's typical of trained models: a few heads are easy to read, and many aren't. Nobody told any head what to do; the jobs come out of training.

Demo · where it stumbles

Looking isn't the same as copying

answer

The years 2080–2099 never appear in training. On "30 May 2073" it reads the 7 and copies it. On "30 May 2093", for the third digit, its attention doesn't land on the 9: it spreads over the 2 and the 0 and writes "0", a year it knows. In training, a year written as "20.." was always followed by 0–7, and this small model seems to lean on that pattern more than on what it reads. Spelled out, "twenty ninety-three" works: the word "ninety" appears in training in years like "nineteen ninety", and the model learned to read it. Part 4's GRU model, on the same exam, copied the digit 99.9% of the time. A good discussion point: neither architecture "understands" years; they generalise in different ways, and the only way to find out is to test on data unlike the training set.

The --max-dates 4 model, live: trained on inputs of 1 to 4 dates. Each row is one character written (tiny, there are 44), each column one character read; the map is block 2, all heads. Same shape as Part 4's: one block per date, marching down the input. Numbers from demo/transformer.py train --max-dates 4 --steps 8000, then test --max-dates 4 (seed 0), 3,000 inputs per column. It needed twice the training rounds of Part 4's model: at 4,000 rounds it was still learning and got 83% on four dates. Each round is quicker, though, so the wall-clock time was similar (about 20 minutes on a laptop CPU). The default input avoids 2080–2099, the unseen years from the previous slide.

One diagram, three families

Keep both halves, or just one

Nearly every model you hear about is one of these three. Encoder–decoder keeps the whole diagram: the original Transformer for translation, and T5, which casts every task as text in, text out. Decoder-only drops the encoder and with it the cross-attention: a stack of masked self-attention blocks that predicts the next word, which is GPT and almost every chatbot today. Encoder-only drops the decoder: every word sees every other word, both sides, and there's no writing; you put a small layer on top for the task. That's BERT, Part 7. A one-line way to remember: the encoder understands, the decoder writes, and the mask is what makes a stack a writer.

Be ready to answer

Questions

  1. Draw the Transformer and name every sublayer. (encoder: self-attention, feed-forward; decoder: masked self-attention, cross-attention, feed-forward; each with add & norm; embeddings + positions below, linear + softmax on top)
  2. In cross-attention, where do the queries, keys and values come from? (queries from the decoder; keys and values from the encoder's output)
  3. What does the feed-forward sublayer add? (non-linear work on each position separately; attention only moves information between positions)
  4. Why residual connections? (blame flows back along the identity path, so deep stacks train; like the LSTM's belt)
  5. What does layer norm normalise over? (the d numbers of one position's vector, then a learned scale and shift)
  6. Why can training run in parallel but writing can't? (training feeds the known answer, shifted right, with a mask; writing needs each character before the next)
  7. Encoder-only, decoder-only, encoder–decoder: one example of each. (BERT; GPT; the original Transformer or T5)
Cover the hints and ask each one cold. Question 1 should be answered by drawing, with the arrow from the encoder's top into the middle of each decoder block.

Recap

Remember:

  1. Encoder block: self-attention, feed-forward. Decoder block: masked self-attention, cross-attention (Part 4's look-back), feed-forward.
  2. Every sublayer: z ← LayerNorm(z + sublayer(z)). The add is a short path for blame; the norm keeps the scale steady.
  3. Training: whole answer in one masked pass. Writing: one pass per character.
Ask someone to draw the full diagram from memory, then label where Part 4's attention lives in it.
